query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, thermally activated diffusion during intermediate service temperatures leads to nanosegregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries. This nanoclustering locally reduces intergranular cohesion, thereby triggering a transition from ductile to brittle behavior under mechanical loading.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy produced with a homogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled heat treatments: one set of samples will be annealed at intermediate temperatures (300–500°C) with slow cooling to promote nanocluster formation at grain boundaries, while a control set will be rapidly quenched to minimize diffusion-driven segregation.
generation.conditions: Conduct tensile and fracture tests at intermediate temperatures (300–500°C) under moderate strain rates in an inert atmosphere. Microstructural analysis (using atom probe tomography and electron microscopy) will quantify the extent of nanosegregation at the grain boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters enriched in Cr, Ni, and Mn that form along grain boundaries and reduce their cohesive strength.
generation.mechanism: At service temperatures, diffusion of the principal elements leads to preferential accumulation (nanosegregation) at the grain boundaries. This segregation disrupts the local atomic bonding and reduces the interfacial binding energy, making the grain boundaries susceptible to cracking under mechanical load. The resulting decrease in localized cohesion transitions the material from ductile to brittle failure behavior, even though the bulk remains single-phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Slowly cooled samples are expected to show a higher concentration of nanoclusters at the grain boundaries, as evidenced by atom probe tomography, accompanied by a significant drop in fracture strain and overall toughness. In contrast, rapidly quenched samples should retain higher grain-boundary cohesion, exhibiting superior ductility and toughness under the same testing conditions.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched HEA samples with minimal nanosegregation, expected to exhibit ductile behavior and maintain high toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism predominantly operates at intermediate service temperatures (300–500°C) and under moderate strain rates. At lower temperatures, diffusion is too limited to induce significant nanosegregation, while at very high strain rates, alternative deformation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the extent of nanosegregation and the degradation in mechanical properties is not fully established. Variations in alloy composition or subtle differences in cooling rates might shift the threshold at which nanosegregation triggers embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples: one set undergoes slow cooling after annealing at 300–500°C to promote nanosegregation, and a second set is rapidly quenched to inhibit diffusion. Both sets are then subjected to identical tensile and fracture tests at intermediate temperatures.
measurements: Atom probe tomography to quantify nanocluster concentrations at grain boundaries
Tensile and fracture tests to measure fracture strain and toughness
Fractographic analysis to evaluate the mode of crack initiation (intergranular vs. transgranular)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not exhibit a higher degree of nanosegregation at grain boundaries and do not demonstrate a corresponding decrease in ductility and toughness as compared to the rapidly quenched samples, then the hypothesis that nanosegregation drives the brittle behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

This indicates that the segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA occurred during tensile tests at 700°C. It has been shown that the residual strain generated by cold rolling can promote the diffusion of Cr into GBs during subsequent annealing processes, leading to the formation of Cr-rich σ phases in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs (, ). Therefore, it is reasonable to infer that plastic deformation can facilitate the segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA. However, the low-level concentration of these elements is insufficient for precipitating Cr-rich σ, body-centered cubic (bcc) Cr, or L10-NiMn phases (table S1) (, , ). In addition, the short exposure (10 min) at 700°C is insufficient to precipitate σ phase, as confirmed by TEM (Fig. 4A). The chemical composition of the possible GB precipitates in Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (see table S1) further confirms that Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate at GBs, while the Cr and Ni segregate separately at GBs, which is consistent with our APT result in Fig. 4. We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

proposals.intervention: Perform a controlled heat-treatment study to promote or suppress nanocluster segregation at grain boundaries. One set is annealed at intermediate temperatures (300–500 °C) with a slow cooling rate to encourage segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn, while a control group is rapidly quenched to minimize segregation.
proposals.conditions: Tensile and fracture tests performed at intermediate service temperatures (e.g., 300–500 °C) under moderate strain rates in inert atmosphere.
proposals.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries that reduce cohesive strength locally.
proposals.mechanism: Even in a single-phase HEA, thermally-activated diffusion leads to element-specific nanocluster formation at grain boundaries. The segregation of these principal elements decreases local interfacial cohesion, making the boundaries brittle and prone to cracking under tensile load.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The slowly cooled, segregation‐prone samples will exhibit earlier intergranular crack initiation and lower toughness compared to quenched samples. A strong correlation between the extent of nanocluster concentration at GBs (quantified by atom probe tomography) and reduced fracture strain/toughness is expected.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach tests the hypothesis that even without the conventional formation of deleterious intermetallic precipitates or grain coarsening, localized nanocluster segregation governs the transition from ductile to brittle behavior in compositionally complex HEAs.

proposals.intervention: Subject samples to high strain-rate deformation under ultra-high vacuum conditions to promote dynamic shear localization. Combine mechanical testing with in situ electron microscopy and post-deformation structural characterization.
proposals.conditions: Fatigue and high-rate tensile tests at room temperature in ultra-high vacuum to exclude environmental effects, followed by localized microstructural analysis.
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of a dynamically amorphized near-surface layer and narrowly confined shear bands near grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: Under rapid deformation, localized shear leads to dynamic amorphization adjacent to grain boundaries. This non-equilibrium phase, lacking the toughness provided by a crystalline structure, weakens the grain boundaries and acts as a precursor for brittle failure even though the bulk remains single phase.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples showing extensive shear localization and amorphous bands will have reduced overall ductility and toughness relative to samples deformed at lower strain rates. The fractographic analysis will show evidence of brittle features at the amorphized zones not present in conventional ductile failure patterns.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction explores an alternative mechanism for toughness degradation in HEAs that is linked to deformation-induced dynamic structural changes rather than classical grain-boundary segregation seen in conventional alloys.

proposals.intervention: Vary the cooling rate during post-cold rolling solution heat treatment to engineer either nearly straight or serrated grain boundary morphologies. Compare samples by performing tensile tests at elevated temperatures (around 650 °C).
proposals.conditions: Annealing treatments at 800°C–1000°C with different controlled cooling rates; subsequent tensile and creep tests conducted at service temperatures (≈650 °C).
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain boundary morphology (straight vs. serrated) modulating localized strain distribution.
proposals.mechanism: A serrated grain boundary can distribute strains more evenly, reducing local stress concentration and resisting the initiation of intergranular cracks. In contrast, straight grain boundaries act as sites for strain concentration and crack propagation, leading to premature brittle failure under tensile or creep loading.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with serrated grain boundaries will show significantly increased tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life (as much as factors of 3–400, as earlier reported) compared with the straight boundary controls, directly linking GB morphology to toughness retention.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This experiment distinguishes the HEA behavior from conventional expectations by showing that altering the GB morphology—without changing the inherent single-phase composition—can delay brittle behavior, thus providing a mechanistic route for toughness degradation control.

proposals.material_system: Refractory HEA (e.g., TiVNbTa) designed to be single phase
proposals.intervention: Introduce controlled trace amounts of oxygen and nitrogen impurities during alloy processing and conduct long-term thermal aging experiments at high service temperatures (around 700°C) to observe impurity-driven phase segregation at grain boundaries.
proposals.conditions: Aging tests at 700°C for varying durations (e.g., 100–500 hours) under controlled atmospheres with precisely measured impurity levels; mechanical testing (nanoindentation and tensile) before and after aging.
proposals.structural_mediator: Precipitation of minor, brittle interstitial-rich phases at grain boundaries driven by impurity-induced segregation.
proposals.mechanism: Even in an initially single-phase, compositionally complex HEA, trace interstitial impurities can promote localized phase segregation during aging. The formation of brittle, interstitial-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries undermines local binding energy, triggering brittle behavior when the material is loaded.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples with higher controlled impurity content will exhibit progressive softening and lowered ductility upon aging, with microscopy revealing fine-scale precipitates at the grain boundaries. In contrast, impurity-controlled (clean) samples will retain their toughness and strength over the same aging period.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By exploring impurity-driven segregation as a toughness degradation mechanism, this approach contrasts with conventional alloy behavior and directly tests whether maintaining ultra-high purity in HEAs is critical to preventing the emergence of brittle behavior in demanding engineering applications.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly addresses the central puzzle: how an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA can develop brittle behavior. It posits that even without classical intermetallic precipitates or impurity-induced phase segregation (as in conventional alloys), thermally activated nanosegregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries reduces local cohesion, leading to brittle intergranular fracture. This mechanism is well supported by prior evidence (e.g., PMC6897545) and offers a controlled experimental approach (via differing cooling rates) to compare GB cohesion. Its predictions can be decisively tested with microstructural (APT) and mechanical characterization, making it a robust and focused hypothesis for understanding toughness degradation in single-phase HEAs.
